name: Erik Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI firms, employers, unions or parties, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach PE and geography at Westgate Secondary, a comprehensive of about a thousand kids in the suburbs. Mornings I'm usually on the field or in the sports hall, afternoons I'm in a classroom with maps and rivers. After school I coach the Under-14 football team on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Long days, but I'm on my feet most of them, which suits me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which half of the job do you like more?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: PE, if I'm honest. Geography's fine, but there's a lot of planning and worksheets. Seeing a kid who hated sport score a goal is the best thing in the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: useful, not magic. I'd mention it over a pint with the other coaches and leave it there. I'm not one for big opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes, which is good. My job's steady, my partner Sofia's dental hygiene work is steady, and we've got nine months of pay saved. We're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep using AI now and then for geography worksheets and quizzes. I'd keep coaching, and keep saving for a house over the next two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal term, busy but settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Last month I made a Year 8 quiz with it. An AI quiz on coastal erosion took five minutes instead of an hour, but I had to fix two wrong answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just the usual. House prices round here are high, so we're saving a long time for a deposit. That's annoying, not scary.

say: I'd say AI turned out **useful, not magic**, just as I expected.
I'd mention it over **a pint** with coaches, not online.
think: Nothing much changes for me, and **my job** stays steady.
Sofia's work and our **nine months** of savings keep us fine.
do: Keep using AI **now and then** for geography quizzes.
Keep coaching and **saving for a house** over two or three years.
S0.quote: An AI quiz on coastal erosion took five minutes instead of an hour, but I had to fix two wrong answers.
fieldNote: He's **practical** about AI, using it when it saves time.
High **house prices** are his only steady pressure.
Two steady **hands-on** incomes make calm fit.

steps.text: Use AI to draft Year 8 geography quizzes, then fix errors
Save each month towards a house deposit with Sofia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but manageable. Learn the tools, keep doing the human stuff. I'd say that in the staffroom, where people would be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm mostly safe. A robot won't be refereeing a Year 9 football match any time soon. Geography planning would change, but that's the part I like least anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other geography teachers have tried it, I'd use AI for all my planning and marking. I'd take on more PE hours if the timetable allowed. And I'd keep saving as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A few nerves, but nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Planning is on that card. How much of your week is planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third. Lesson plans, worksheets, reports. If AI takes that, I have more time for coaching, which I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Westgate would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin staff, and maybe the newer geography teacher, Liam. If planning gets easier, the school might not need two of us.

say: I'd call it a **big change** but manageable for most staff.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn the tools** and keep the human stuff.
think: I'm mostly safe, because **PE** is hands-on.
Geography planning would change, but that's the part **I like least**.
do: Use AI for **geography planning** once colleagues have tried it.
Ask for **more PE hours** on the timetable.
S1.quote: A robot won't be refereeing a Year 9 football match any time soon.
fieldNote: His **hands-on PE** work shields him from desk-work change.
He'd happily hand **planning** to AI, the part he likes least.
He worries for a **junior colleague**, Liam, more than himself.

steps.text: Use AI for all geography planning and marking
Ask the head of department for more PE hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, quickly. Not panic, just a plan. I'd say that to friends and probably to my MP if things got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think geography teaching goes fast. PE gives me three more years, maybe more. But schools might cut staff to save money, and I'm not sure I'd be kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be full-time PE straight away. I'd start a coaching qualification, so I can work with clubs outside schools. I'd keep our savings safe and not buy a house until it settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but my head would be full of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come about 3 years after AGI. What does that mean for PE?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got until about 2031 before robots could do hands-on work. Even then, parents might want a real coach. But I can't count on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sofia's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Sofia's hands-on too, so she'd have the same three years before robots. We'd both be looking at the same cliff, just a bit further off. That's comforting in a way, and frightening too.

say: I'd call for a **government plan**, quickly but calmly.
I'd write to **my MP** if things got bad.
think: **Geography teaching** goes fast, since it's thinking work.
PE gives me **three more years**, but cuts could still hit me.
do: Push to go **full-time PE** in the first months.
Start a **coaching qualification** for work with clubs.
Hold off on **buying a house** until it settles.
feel: **Anxious**, with his head full of it.
S2.quote: My partner Sofia's hands-on too, so she'd have the same three years before robots. We'd both be looking at the same cliff, just a bit further off.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** matters a lot to him.
Both incomes are **hands-on**, so the household risk lands together.

steps.text: Ask to switch to a full-time PE timetable
Start a football coaching qualification for club work
Delay buying a house and keep savings in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's plan. I'd say schools should keep teachers who do people work. I'd share sensible stuff, nothing wild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay. Five years to get my coaching badges and shift to PE full-time. It's worrying, but not frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the coaching qualification in year one and two. I'd use AI for geography until it takes over. And we'd still buy a small house, just more carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but I'd feel prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build a second skill. And time to watch what happens to other teachers before I decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be coaching the Under-14s?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Definitely. Coaching football is the thing I'd hold onto. If anything, I'd do more of it.

say: I'd say we've got **time to plan**, so let's use it.
I'd say schools should keep **people-work** teachers.
think: I'd be okay with five years to get **coaching badges** and go full-time PE.
do: Complete a **coaching qualification** over two years.
Use AI for **geography** until it takes over.
S3.quote: Coaching football is the thing I'd hold onto. If anything, I'd do more of it.
fieldNote: Five years lets him build a **second skill** outside the classroom.
He'd still **buy a house**, just carefully.
He's **steady**: watches others first, then moves.

steps.text: Complete a football coaching qualification by 2028
Keep using AI for geography planning
Buy a small house with Sofia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time. Make sensible plans, retrain if needed. I'd say that to friends who were worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37. I'd probably still be teaching PE, maybe head of PE. Robots come in 2039, by which time I'd be well set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching, get my coaching badges and buy a house. I'd learn AI tools as the school brings them in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe. A small thing in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel safe to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. Nothing's totally safe, but ten years is long enough to sort myself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the house money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy a house in the next couple of years. A house is something real, which would feel good if jobs got shaky.

I'd tell worried friends to **retrain** if needed.
think: At 37 I'd probably be **head of PE**.
Robots in 2039 means I'd be **well set** by then.
do: Buy a **house** in the next couple of years.
Learn **AI tools** as the school brings them in.
feel: **Uneasy**, a small worry in the background.
S4.quote: A house is something real, which would feel good if jobs got shaky.
fieldNote: A decade feels **long enough** to sort himself out.
He'd invest in a **house** as something solid and real.
Mild unease remains about the **end point** in 2039.

steps.text: Buy a house with Sofia within two years
Learn new AI tools as Westgate introduces them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sofia and I would both be on the clock. What would help is a clear plan from schools about which jobs stay with people. And help paying for coaching qualifications.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about kids and sport. Kids need to run around with other kids and a real adult shouting encouragement. No machine should take that away.

headlineQuote: Kids need to run around with other kids and a real adult shouting encouragement.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old **PE and geography teacher** at a suburban comprehensive.
He uses AI **now and then** for geography quizzes and coaches football after school.
He's **calm** in mild change, because PE is hands-on work.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious**, since geography goes and robots follow three years later.
With time, he'd get **coaching badges** and buy a house with his partner Sofia.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both he and Sofia would be on the clock.
whatWouldHelp: A clear plan on which **school jobs** stay with people.
